title: Smart watches and glasses no longer allowed in Manitoba schools
summary: Smart glasses, smart watches and other wearable technologies are now included in the ban on cellphones in schools that has been in place since September 2024, says the Manitoba government.

image.caption: Smart watches are now included in the school ban that initially applied only to cellphones in Manitoba. (Markus Schreiber/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Manitoba·New
Smart glasses, smart watches and other wearable technologies are now included in the ban on cellphones in schools that has been in place since September 2024, says the Manitoba government.
Wearable technologies now included in cellphone ban
Education Minister Tracy Schmidt sent a directive to school leaders last week, telling them to include the devices in their cellphone ban.
"As technology evolves, so must our guidelines to ensure students are learning in healthy, safe environments that support their education and well-being," Schmidt said in a statement sent to the CBC.

The intent of the original cellphone ban was "to reduce distractions in classrooms and minimize the harmful impacts associated with social media and online platforms," said the Nov. 17 letter, which was sent to all school division superintendents as well as principals of independent schools that receive public funding.

"As technology continues to evolve, students increasingly have access to a wide range of personal devices … that allow access to messaging, social media, internet browsing, photography, audio or video recording, artificial intelligence tools, or other cellphone-like functions can create many of the same distractions and harms that cellphones cause."
Meta smart glasses have built-in artificial intelligence, cameras, speakerphones, microphones and touch controls. (Shane Fowler/CBC)
The directive was issued one week after Hanover School Division became the first in the province to ban smart glasses in its schools.
A letter sent to parents by the division in southeast Manitoba cited privacy implications because "they can record audio and video without others readily knowing."
A Canadian media literacy expert said Manitoba is on the right track, but she would like to see rules established on a federal level.

"What we don't want to end up with is a sort of patchwork of 13 different provinces and territories trying to regulate this in a sort of different shade of grey, if you will, around the same kind of technological challenge," said Kara Brisson-Boivin, director of research at Mediasmarts, a digital media literacy advocacy group based in Ottawa.

As technology evolves, students increasingly have access to a range of personal devices that offer the same functions as cellphones, and can cause the same distractions and harms as cellphones, Brisson-Boivin said.

Meta, one of several makers of AI glasses, says on its website that its product includes an LED light that blinks to alert others the wearer is taking a picture or recording video, and the glasses will automatically disable the camera if they detect the capture light was covered or tampered with.

"That's difficult to recognize, especially when we're talking about children and youth. We have to teach a lot of privacy-forward practices that are increasingly difficult to do, with especially younger children," Brisson-Boivin said.

Wearable devices that 'allow access to messaging, social media, internet browsing, photography, audio or video recording, artificial intelligence tools, or other cellphone-like functions' can create the same distractions as cellphones, Manitoba Education Minister Tracy Schmidt says. (Steffi Loos/The Associated Press)

The subject of the recording also has to notice the light, and online criticism says the LEDs are small and easy to miss in direct sunlight and even bright indoor lighting, from the side or in crowded spaces.
While Brisson-Boivin appreciates Manitoba's efforts around wearable tech, she doesn't believe policing it should fall on the shoulders of teachers and other school staff.
"Educators are already so overwrought and overrun with all of their day-to-day challenges that placing an additional challenge of managing new tech … is really difficult to do," she said.
She's also not convinced a blanket long-term ban is the right way to go.
The drawbacks to the tech are clear but consideration needs to be given to those who rely on it, Brisson-Boivin said.

blocks.text: Students with visual impairments and hearing impairments could be aided by it, "but we don't know enough yet about the potential benefits," she said.
"It makes good sense to want to slow down the integration of new forms of technology, to be able to do it in a way that feels controlled, that we sort of study the benefits as well as the harms.”
Taking advantage of any potential benefits must be done with the proper protections in place, she said.

There must be regulations that hold developers accountable for privacy considerations and a support around education on "how, when and where to use the technology" and when not to, Brisson-Boivin said.
"Manitoba is taking important steps, but I think that we need to have a broader conversation across the country about the role and the place of wearable technology," she said.
"AI, like any other technology, is a tool, and tools can be used to hone our skills, but we don't want those tools to be used to replace our skills."

Darren Bernhardt has been with CBC Manitoba since 2009 and specializes in offbeat and local history stories. He is the author of two bestselling books: The Lesser Known: A History of Oddities from the Heart of the Continent, and Prairie Oddities: Punkinhead, Peculiar Gravity and More Lesser Known Histories.
